title: Understanding HOA Special Assessments Before Buying a Home
content_html:
Many homes in Temecula Valley, Murrieta, and Menifee sit within a homeowners association, and most buyers already know to budget for the monthly or quarterly HOA dues. Fewer buyers think ahead about special assessments — the one-time (or sometimes recurring) charges an association can levy on top of regular dues. Understanding how these assessments work, and how to research the risk before you close, can save you from an unpleasant surprise after move-in.

What Is an HOA Special Assessment?

Regular HOA dues are meant to cover routine, predictable costs: landscaping, common-area utilities, insurance, management fees, and contributions to a reserve fund for future repairs. A special assessment is a separate charge the board levies when those regular funds aren't enough to cover a specific need — often an unplanned or larger-than-expected expense.

Common triggers include:

  • A major repair the reserve fund wasn't large enough to cover, such as roof replacement, pool resurfacing, or structural repairs to a shared building component
  • Storm, fire, or other casualty damage not fully covered by the association's insurance
  • Litigation costs, including construction-defect disputes or disputes with contractors
  • Capital improvements the membership votes to add, like gate systems, clubhouse upgrades, or new amenities
  • A reserve study that reveals the association has been underfunding long-term maintenance for years

Special assessments can be a single lump-sum bill, or spread across several months or years depending on the size of the expense and the association's governing documents.

Why This Matters Before You Buy, Not After

A special assessment isn't tied to how long you've owned the home — it's tied to ownership at the time the assessment is levied or becomes due, depending on the association's rules and the purchase contract's allocation of the cost. That means a buyer who closes shortly before a large assessment is approved can end up responsible for some or all of it, even though the underlying deferred maintenance built up long before they owned the property.

This is also a useful lens for evaluating the overall financial health of an association. A community with a history of frequent or large special assessments, or a reserve fund that's chronically underfunded, is telling you something about how well it's been managed — information that's just as relevant to your long-term costs as the listed sale price.

Where to Find This Information During Escrow

California law gives HOA buyers a structured way to review an association's finances before the purchase becomes final. When you buy a home in a common interest development, the seller (or the association, depending on the document) is required to provide a packet of HOA disclosure documents, which typically includes:

  • The association's governing documents (CC&Rs, bylaws, and rules)
  • Current financial statements and the operating budget
  • The reserve study and reserve fund balance
  • Minutes from recent board meetings
  • Any pending or recently approved special assessments
  • Information about pending litigation involving the association

Reading the reserve study and recent board minutes carefully is often more informative than reading the CC&Rs themselves — board minutes in particular tend to surface discussions about upcoming repairs or funding shortfalls well before a formal assessment vote happens. If anything in the packet is unclear, your purchase agreement likely includes a contingency period during which you can ask questions, request clarification, or in some cases cancel the transaction based on what you learn. For a broader look at how contingencies work in a California purchase contract, see our guide to purchase agreement contingencies.

Questions Worth Asking Before You Remove Contingencies

  • Has the association levied a special assessment in the past several years, and if so, for what?
  • Is a special assessment currently pending, proposed, or under board discussion?
  • What does the most recent reserve study say about the percentage of reserves funded relative to projected need?
  • Are there any known deferred maintenance items — roofs, paving, pool equipment, irrigation, shared structures — that haven't yet been addressed?
  • Is the association involved in any lawsuit, and could that lawsuit result in a future assessment?

Your real estate agent and, where appropriate, a real estate attorney can help you interpret what you're reading in the disclosure packet. A home inspector can also flag visible deferred maintenance in common areas that might foreshadow a future assessment, even if nothing has been formally proposed yet.

How Special Assessments Differ From Regular Dues Increases

It's worth distinguishing a special assessment from a routine increase in monthly dues. Dues increases are usually modest, recurring adjustments tied to rising operating costs, and boards typically have more routine authority to adjust them within the association's governing documents. Special assessments are usually larger, tied to a specific expense, and may require a membership vote or board approval process spelled out in the CC&Rs or under the Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act, California's primary statutory framework governing HOAs. If you're evaluating an HOA community generally — not just the assessment risk — it's worth reading our companion piece on understanding HOA fees before you buy in a planned community, and our guide to how HOA board elections and voting rights work under the Davis-Stirling Act, since the same board that controls elections typically controls assessment votes.

Negotiating Around a Known Assessment

If you learn during escrow that a special assessment has already been approved, or is clearly imminent, this becomes a negotiating point like any other material fact uncovered during the transaction. Buyers sometimes ask the seller to pay the assessment before closing, to credit it at closing, or to adjust the purchase price to account for it. Whether any of this is achievable depends on market conditions, the specific language of your purchase agreement, and how the assessment is structured (one-time payment vs. an installment plan that runs with the property vs. one that runs with the owner at time of levy). This is exactly the kind of detail worth raising with your agent as soon as the HOA disclosure packet arrives, rather than waiting until closer to closing.

The Bottom Line for Buyers

An HOA special assessment isn't automatically a reason to walk away from a home you otherwise like — many well-run associations never need one, and others use them appropriately to fund a genuinely necessary improvement. The goal isn't to avoid every community that has ever levied one; it's to go in with clear eyes about the association's financial condition, read the disclosure packet closely, ask direct questions, and factor what you learn into your decision and your offer.
